Consider the following statements about Parliament's amending power and the courts:

1. The 42nd Amendment Act (1976) recast Article 368 so that Parliament's constituent power was stated to be without limit.
2. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Golak Nath and upheld the validity of the 24th Amendment Act (1971).
3. The doctrine of the basic structure was first laid down by the Supreme Court in the Golak Nath case (1967).
4. The Supreme Court is yet to define what constitutes the basic structure; the basic features have emerged from various judgements.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Chapter 12 (p.199). Statement 2 is correct: Chapter 12 (p.198). Statement 3 is incorrect: Golak Nath held Fundamental Rights beyond amendment; the basic structure doctrine was laid down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) (p.198). Statement 4 is correct: Chapter 12 (p.199). So exactly 3 of the 4 statements are correct.
w: 'Only two' miscounts: the statements checked one by one give exactly 3 correct.
'All four' miscounts: the statements checked one by one give exactly 3 correct.
'Only one' miscounts: the statements checked one by one give exactly 3 correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Article 34:

1. It empowers Parliament to indemnify any government servant or other person for any act done in connection with the maintenance or restoration of order in an area under martial law.
2. A court can strike down Parliament's Act of Indemnity if it infringes a Fundamental Right.
3. Article 34 itself supplies a definition of martial law.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Chapter text. Statement 2 is incorrect: It cannot be so challenged. Statement 3 is incorrect: It is not defined anywhere in the Constitution. So exactly 1 of the 3 statements are correct.
w: 'None' miscounts: the statements checked one by one give exactly 1 correct.
'Only two' miscounts: the statements checked one by one give exactly 1 correct.
'All three' miscounts: the statements checked one by one give exactly 1 correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: The enforcement of the right to life under Article 21 can be suspended by a Presidential Order during a National Emergency.
Statement-II: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 barred the suspension of the right to move the court for the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
o: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
questions.e: Statement-I is incorrect: after the 44th Amendment the President cannot suspend the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 (Laxmikanth p.263). Statement-II is correct and is the very reason Statement-I is false.
w: Rejected: Statement-I is incorrect, since Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended after the 44th Amendment, so the pair cannot both be correct.
Rejected: Statement-I is incorrect, so there is no pair of correct statements, whatever the link between them.
Rejected: Statement-II is correct (the 44th Amendment protects Articles 20 and 21), so calling it incorrect fails.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: After Kesavananda Bharati, Parliament may amend a Fundamental Right, but not one that forms part of the basic structure.
Statement-II: In the Golak Nath case (1967) the Supreme Court had held that an amending Act is also a 'law' under Article 13 and is therefore void if it violates a Fundamental Right.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Statement-I is correct (Laxmikanth p.198): Kesavananda allowed Parliament to abridge Fundamental Rights, but not a right that forms part of the basic structure. Statement-II is correct (p.198), but it describes the earlier ruling that Kesavananda overruled; it is not the reason for the post-Kesavananda position, so II does not explain I.
w: Rejected: Golak Nath's position was overruled by Kesavananda, so it cannot be the reason for the current position.
Rejected: Statement-II is correct; it states the Golak Nath position (1967) accurately (p.198).
Rejected: Statement-I is correct; after Kesavananda Parliament may abridge a right short of the basic structure (p.198).

questions.q:
Pair each judgment in List-I with its significance in List-II.

List-I
A. Minerva Mills case (1980)
B. Waman Rao case (1980)
C. I.R. Coelho case (2007)
D. Central Coal Fields case (1980)

List-II
1. No blanket immunity from judicial review for Ninth Schedule laws
2. Invalidated the 42nd Amendment's declaration that Parliament's amending power was without limit, as it excluded judicial review
3. Effective access to justice as a basic feature
4. Basic structure applies to amendments enacted after 24 April 1973
questions.e: Minerva Mills invalidated the 42nd Amendment's recast of Article 368 (p.199); Waman Rao fixed the 24 April 1973 date (p.199); I.R. Coelho denied blanket immunity to Ninth Schedule laws (p.166); Central Coal Fields lists effective access to justice in Table 12.1 (p.201).
w: 'A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3' swaps A and B: Minerva Mills struck the 42nd Amendment's Article 368 clause; Waman Rao dealt with the date.
'A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3' swaps B and C: Waman Rao fixed the date, Coelho the Ninth Schedule point.
'A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1' swaps C and D: Coelho is about the Ninth Schedule, Central Coal Fields about access to justice.
